item.title: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
item.description:
After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies failed to win an outright majority in last month’s Israeli election, he insisted the vote was stolen, arguing that record turnout by Arab voters was part of a conspiracy to rig the result.

As evidence for his claims, Mr. Netanyahu seized on the arrests of three activists for Raam, an Arab-led opposition party, on the morning of Election Day. The Israeli police said at the time that the men were believed to have been planning to bribe voters, adding that officers had seized envelopes of cash that might have been part of a plot.

Raam denied the allegations, and the activists were ultimately released without charge. But what Mr. Netanyahu did not say at the time was that his own chief of staff and a former aide had been involved in the initial outreach to the police that led to the arrests.

Both aides acknowledged their involvement this week. The suggestion that Mr. Netanyahu’s office had a hand in the arrests of his political opponents has prompted calls for an investigation. The Israeli attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, said on Tuesday that she and the state prosecutor were looking into the matter.

Ram Ben Barak, a centrist lawmaker from the opposition Together party and a former deputy chief of the Mossad intelligence agency, said that the allegations evoked repressive states such as President Vladimir V. Putin’s Russia, in which the police are weaponized as a political tool.

“I would never have imagined that this kind of story would emerge from the Israeli prime minister’s office,” Mr. Ben Barak added.

Mr. Netanyahu’s aides initially denied reports, including in The New York Times, that the police who arrested the three Raam activists on Oct. 27 were acting on a telephone tip provided by the prime minister’s chief of staff, Ido Norden. But on Sunday, after an investigative report by the Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 unearthed new details about the episode, Mr. Netanyahu’s office changed course.

“Criminal information reached Ido Norden, the chief of staff,” his office said in a statement. “He carried out his duty, like any other citizen.”

After an election that left neither Mr. Netanyahu nor the opposition with a clear path to forming a government, critics of the prime minister say the episode shows how far he will go to maintain his grip on power. They also say it reinforces fears that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies have bent Israel’s security agencies to serve their personal agendas, which the prime minister has denied.

The Israeli prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for further comment, nor did the Israeli police or the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency.

On the morning that Israelis headed to the polls, Mr. Netanyahu trumpeted news of the arrests in bluntly racial terms, appealing to right-wing Jewish Israelis to vote because more Arabs were voting than Jews.

“This is an emergency appeal,” he said. “They are trying to steal the elections from us.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party secured more seats in Israel’s Parliament, the Knesset, than any other, even though the opposition parties collectively have a majority.

Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the opposition Yashar party and is Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, has demanded a criminal investigation into the arrests. He has accused Mr. Netanyahu of potentially “planting evidence and deploying the police against Arab citizens of Israel without valid search or arrest warrants.”

The surge in turnout among Arab voters handed the Arab-led parties a historic 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset. After the vote, Mr. Netanyahu initiated an aggressive push to delegitimize the results, at times echoing President Trump’s “stop the steal” campaign after the 2020 U.S. elections.

Israeli election officials have repeatedly said there is no proof of widespread fraud that could affect the results. That has not deterred Likud, which continues to assert that the election was tainted, warning in a statement that the Arab parties would bring about “the Islamification of Israel.”

Raam, the party of the three arrested activists, is a pragmatic Arab-led grouping with Islamist roots. It is one of the two main Arab parties in Israel. Portraying Raam as being linked with possible criminality has some benefit for Mr. Netanyahu as it could complicate any effort by Mr. Eisenkot to form a coalition that relied on the Arab party’s support.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, is separately investigating potential foreign funding in the election — an inquiry that Likud has also invoked to assert that the vote was flawed. But the investigation has not found any widespread bribery or tampering with the election results, Noam Sohlberg, a conservative judge who chairs the Central Elections Committee, said on Tuesday.

Now, after the revelations about the initial contact with the police, Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals say that the real meddling on Election Day may have been perpetrated by the prime minister’s associates.

On Monday, Israel’s national broadcaster, Kan, named the tipster as Daniel Greenberg, who worked in Mr. Netanyahu’s office from 2023 until a few months ago. In a government document, reviewed by The Times, Mr. Greenberg is described as an “adviser on Arab affairs.”

A lawyer for Mr. Greenberg, Avichai Yehosef, confirmed in an interview that his client was the source of the tip, but denied that he had tried to improperly influence the election, saying that Mr. Greenberg had merely passed along information about the activists’ intention to bribe voters.

Mr. Yehosef said that Mr. Greenberg had learned the names of the three Raam activists from an Arab lawmaker. He declined to name the lawmaker.

The three Raam activists were arrested before dawn on Election Day, Oct. 27, at their homes in southern Israel, court filings show. At least two of their homes were searched without warrants, the police later admitted in court.

One of the activists, Dr. Sayyaf Abu Riash, 38, said in an interview that he woke up at roughly 4:30 a.m. that day when the police demanded to enter and search his home. Officers refused to say what they were looking for, Dr. Abu Riash said, before telling him to accompany them to a police station, where he was interrogated him about his involvement in the party.

Dr. Abu Riash said that he campaigned on behalf of Raam but did not hold a formal role. He said Israeli leaders should look favorably on Arab citizens turning out in such high numbers.

“It shows that they feel like they’re part of the country,” he said.

Instead, he said that his arrest had been “used to inspire fear” about the prospect of Arab citizens exercising their democratic rights.

Judge Merav Amar Cohen, who ordered Dr. Abu Riash’s release, criticized the police, saying officers had lacked an evidentiary basis to hold him.

“The investigation files show that the defendant is involved in advocating for the Raam party and even involved in house meetings with candidates,” she wrote in a judgment ordering his release. “But that’s not a crime.”

item.title: COP31 Climate Talks Are Bigger Than Ever, but Few Are There to Negotiate
item.description:
There’s a paradox at the center of this year’s United Nations climate conference.

The event is bigger than ever, as tens of thousands of lanyard-wearing participants stream in every morning, grab free apples and chocolate at the entrance, and then proceed to pack every corridor of a gargantuan expo center.

But the end result is expected to be modest, if not marginal.

George Hussey, an Irish attendee, surveyed the crowds this week amid the echo of competing climate panels, and posed what has become a common question.

“What is all this for?” he asked.

Decades ago, the work to address climate change consisted of smallish, technical affairs. But the conferences have boomed into both trade shows and networking events, offering chances to lobby, brainstorm and even commiserate.

This year’s 12-day conference, known as COP31 and held in Antalya, Turkey, seemingly marks the completion of this transformation. Only about 20 percent of the record 92,000 registered participants are there for the formal negotiations.

Many attendees wonder whether the crowds are excessive or whether they prove climate change’s salience even as it appeared to have slipped as a priority in a world focused on conflicts, A.I. and economic problems. Either way, an event often judged for a single formal outcome now consists of thousands of outcomes, as specific as the people in attendance.

“Everybody has their own piece of the puzzle here that they’re interested in,” said Mr. Hussey, a member of Ireland’s Climate Change Advisory Council.

The participants this year include environmental insurance experts, American law students, advocates for sustainable aviation fuels, and one man wearing a Santa hat saying SustainaClaus. Some came for an “Olympics” on building energy savings.

Daniel Cusworth, an American scientist at Carbon Mapper, pitched tools to governments that could uncover large sources of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Carlos Garcia, a Mexican filmmaker, screened a short documentary on landfills, rendered vividly enough to see the flies through 3-D glasses. Bashiir Mohamed, the leader of a Somali green energy association, came to rally funding so that 100,000 homes could obtain solar panels, and with it the chance to power phones, refrigerators and air-conditioning units.

“Energy changes everything,” Mr. Mohamed said.

There’s been plenty of sentiment that the annual climate conference has grown beyond its purpose. The event’s carbon footprint has increased 25-fold over three decades. Two years ago, 22 environmental leaders and scientists wrote a letter to the United Nations calling for streamlining the event with “smaller, more frequent, solution-driven meetings.”

But Johan Rockström, a Swedish scientist who signed the letter, says he has had second thoughts. The big gatherings “manifest to the world that this is something to take seriously,” he said. And they have meaning to the participants, too. For almost two weeks, people work long hours in what can feel like “planetary-scale therapy sessions.”

His only reservation: that the good feeling might be unearned.

“We are still able to tell ourselves that we have done everything we can,” said Dr. Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. “Is this a way for the climate community to feel less frustrated?”

Advocates for the U.N. process note that it has made some key progress. Global temperatures had once been projected to rise almost 4 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels. With nations’ commitments under the Paris climate agreement in 2015, plus the spread of renewable energy, warming is now on track for 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) if current policies continue.

Over the years, COP organizers have set up — and enlarged — an agenda outside of the formal negotiations for voluntary measures from nations, cities, businesses and investors.

Whereas formal negotiations used to be the centerpiece, now “it’s just a little dot in the middle,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of Climate Analytics, a climate science and policy institute based in Berlin.

This year, for instance, negotiators are again fighting over references to fossil fuels in a final agreement, with oil-producing countries capable of blocking any deal in the consensus-based process. But on the sidelines, there have been dozens of events devoted to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, and a handful of nations announced new domestic pledges.

Those hints of momentum, plus being around like-minded people, “makes COP really fulfilling, even if on a bigger level it’s a pretty dire situation we’re facing,” said Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, an independent research organization.

There are a handful of reasons this year’s COP grew so large. Turkey is a convenient destination from Europe, Asia and Africa. Antalya, the host city, has an ample supply of hotel rooms. And Turkey has padded the list with 14,000 guests — civil servants, academics and politicians. COP31 is more than twice the size of last year’s event, held in a Brazilian city on the edge of the rainforest, where organizers used cruise ships to ease hotel room shortages.

It helps that this year’s climate talks have taken place under near-ideal conditions, at least after Turkey fixed transportation chaos that plagued the first days.

Every day, the temperatures have risen to almost exactly 70 degrees. The expo, for all its scale, has plenty of charming touches: work stands where locals draw calligraphy and whittle wooden spinning tops and a domed food court where speakers play fake birdsong. An ornamental water channel cuts through the event halls, zigzagging around coffee shops. (One participant, inevitably, fell in.)

“The venue is great,” said Gerald Miles, an Australian conservationist and longtime COP attendee who was fine-tuning a speech near a pagoda. Among the highlights? “The apples and chocolate,” he said.

Mr. Hussey, of Ireland, said he has concluded that attending COP was a bit like “being back in school.” Everywhere he looked, there was something to learn. As he spoke, one of Ireland’s former presidents walked by. Then its climate and energy minister.

“Unfortunately, no matter how long you stay here, you can only tap a little,” Mr. Hussey said. “You wouldn’t want to live your life in this weird place. It’s not natural. But a little bit every year. You realize, we’re not on our own here.”

item.title: Major Powers Vow to Increase Oil Supply Amid Global Energy Transition
item.description:
Among the four points the leaders of China, Russia and the United States agreed to on Thursday was a promise to work together to increase the production and supply of “refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Their resolve is striking for a few reasons.

The wars led by two of them — Russia and the United States — have caused global oil prices to spike, creating a lot of economic pain for oil-importing nations. That has in turn accelerated their transition away from imported fossil fuel energy sources.

Electric vehicle sales have increased in many major markets, except the United States. And the International Energy Agency recently projected in an annual report that the world would add renewable energy capacity, led by solar, far faster over the next five years than it had in recent years because of what it called “unprecedented disruptions to global energy markets since the outbreak of the Iran war.”

“Renewables, already expanding at a record pace before the current energy crisis, are set to see strong growth across a wider range of countries around the world in the coming years as governments seek to strengthen energy security and reduce their exposure to imported fuels and volatile prices,” the agency said.

On Thursday, in its Energy Outlook Report, the agency went further, concluding that the war against Iran had permanently altered the appetite in many countries for imported oil, especially for oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors.

How would the United States, Russia and China would increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products? That remains unclear. All three nations are refining powerhouses. But Russia’s refineries have been damaged in recent months by Ukrainian attacks. A significant amount of Russian crude oil is now being imported and refined in other countries, including China and India.

These three big countries have different agendas for how the world will be powered in the coming years. Russia and the United States are among the world’s biggest oil producers. They want fossil fuels to remain the main energy source of the global economy. China is leading the world to a very different energy future, one that relies on solar, wind, batteries and battery-powered vehicles for energy — all of which China dominates.

It is also striking that Thursday’s joint statement comes during global climate talks, where most countries (except the United States) have been discussing how to slow down global climate change, which is mainly driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

item.title: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
item.description:
President Trump used his first-ever trilateral summit with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday to say that their respective nations were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth.”

But after an 80-minute conversation at a lakeside villa in the city of Shenzhen, a Chinese technology hub, it was unclear whether the three leaders had agreed to return to the kind of arms control talks that for decades were a centerpiece of diplomacy among superpowers during the Cold War. On new threats, including artificial intelligence, the three leaders were largely silent.

Mr. Trump, who also met with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin separately at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum this week, appeared delighted to convene the world’s largest nuclear powers for a discussion about disarmament. But he did not come with a detailed plan for how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons, or outline a path to one.

Instead, Mr. Trump relished what amounted to a high-profile photo opportunity of the three leaders seated around a circular wooden table. For Mr. Trump, the main achievement seemed to be a mutual commitment to keep talking about peace — without taking meaningful steps toward it.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.” Mr. Trump told Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”

While China, which has the fastest-growing nuclear arsenal on earth, agreed to participate in the three-way discussion of nuclear weapons, the leaders announced little concrete beyond agreeing to continue a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Mr. Xi has long been reluctant to agree to nuclear arms control because China’s arsenal remains a fraction the size of those belonging to Russia and the United States.

In the end, Mr. Trump’s whirlwind journey — two weeks after the Republican Party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections and amid anxiety at home about widespread digital outages — amounted to a grand show of camaraderie.

As host of the tightly choreographed event, Mr. Xi flattered Mr. Trump and gave him an opportunity to ask for China’s assistance on matters ranging from ending global conflicts to spending more on U.S. agricultural goods. The summit also removed Mr. Putin from his status a global pariah over his invasion of Ukraine, elevating him to a leader deserving of equal diplomatic footing.

But for all of the talk of peace, there was no announcement of breakthroughs in the talks the Trump administration is engaged in to end that conflict. Nor did Mr. Trump appear to dwell on finding a way out of the its war with Iran.

“We don’t need any help,” Mr. Trump said, when asked by a Fox News reporter before the summit whether he would seek assistance from the other leaders in ending a conflict of his own making. In fact, the help Mr. Trump could ask for would involve demanding that China and Russia stop assisting Iran: U.S. intelligence has concluded that both countries provided either technology or targeting information that likely helped the Iranians strike American military bases in the Middle East.

On Fox News, Mr. Trump described the three-way conversation as a way to disrupt the growing “partnership without limits” that Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin say they have formed in recent years. Mr. Trump said that he hoped to break up that alignment and turn it into a three-way conversation, rather than a partnership focused on countering American influence.

China and Russia’s alignment, Mr. Trump said, “should have never been allowed to happen.”

Seeking his own path into Mr. Xi’s good graces, Mr. Trump has held three meetings with the Chinese leader this year, with the goal of cooling a tit-for-tat trade war and of building up a personal relationship through mutual flattery. Mr. Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews to welcome Mr. Xi to Washington in May, and Mr. Xi responded in kind when Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, treating the president to a military exercise and a fleet of U.S. and Chinese flag-waving dancers in a flurry of pink, blue and white outfits.

In Shenzhen, the heart of China’s robotics, telecommunications, semiconductor and software industries, Mr. Trump did not visit the chief technological competitors to the United States, or see coffee-serving robots near the city’s center.

Still, he marveled over the ceremonial welcome and held it up as evidence of a warming bond, telling an interviewer that “one of the great presidents of China” had greeted him. “He’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Mr. Trump said.

The president, who spends much of his time in the United States on bombastic appearances and incendiary social media posts, was on his best behavior alongside Mr. Xi. (He was his old self on Fox News before the summit, when he threatened to wipe out Iran should it attack the United States directly.)

Mr. Xi, for his part, said a much improved relationship between China and the United States in recent months was “the right way” for the two powers to “get along.” But he also warned that the key to keeping ties stable “lies in taking concrete actions to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state.” The remarks came days after Washington moved to close a loophole on Chinese access to advanced A.I. chips.

As for Mr. Putin, the summit was his first encounter with Mr. Trump since the two men met in Alaska last year. That meeting was a diplomatic flop, and the war in Ukraine has intensified since then. The peace mechanism Mr. Trump advocated — a direct meeting between Mr. Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, moderated by Mr. Trump — has yet to materialize.

This time, White House officials were modest in their predictions. Expectations were set so low that White House officials who previewed the trip last week initially said that Mr. Trump would not bring up the war in Ukraine at all, although he ultimately did.

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump continued welcoming Russia back into the fold of great superpowers. He called Mr. Putin “my friend,” and insisted that all three leaders would like to see the war end quickly. The Russian leader reiterated after the meeting, however, that he would not be negotiating with Ukraine.

During the trilateral meeting, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin embraced the idea of peaceful leadership, without making commitments that would be much of a burden to either of their countries. In his own remarks, Mr. Putin said that their nations were “united not only by the status of being the victorious countries in World War II, but most importantly by the joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.”

And Mr. Xi mentioned a utopian goal that has pretty much fallen off the agenda of superpowers. He described nuclear weapons as a “sword of Damocles hanging over humanity” that should be eliminated. But Beijing has typically called on the United States to take the first steps in arms control, a demand that Mr. Trump seemed to acknowledge earlier in the day.

“For me, it’s a hard thing,” he told Fox News. “And it’s probably hard for them to do also.”

It has been done before, by Mr. Trump’s predecessors. Today, the United States and Russia each have slightly more than 5,000 nuclear warheads, and only 1,550 deployed under the New Start treaty that expired earlier this year — down from tens of thousands on both sides during the Cold War.

China, however, was never a party to past nuclear reduction treaties, and it is now intent on building up to at least current Russian and U.S. levels.

Mr. Trump also said in Shenzen that he wanted to crack down on nuclear proliferation by smaller powers — his justification for attacking Iran — and restrain what he said were the excesses of “rogue” organizations like the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Putin is subject to an I.C.C. arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Nevertheless Mr. Trump welcomed the Russian leader in Alaska last year and extending an invitation to the Group of 20 summit next month in Florida. Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting that he was unsure if he would attend.

One topic that went missing from each leader’s remarks was artificial intelligence, as China and the United States are locked in fierce competition over the new technology.

Mr. Trump did not answer a question, shouted by a Bloomberg News reporter at APEC earlier in the day, if the former chief executive of Nvidia — a company that has been central to the A.I. boom — had been disloyal to the United States. The executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after he was found to have two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset.

The reporter who shouted the question was admonished by Chinese officials and barred from the trilateral meeting. Mr. Trump seemed blasé about the matter of espionage earlier in the day, telling Fox News that “we spy on them too.”

As the president basked in flattery from an authoritarian whose iron-fisted leadership he has openly admired, he gently suggested that he had not received as much media coverage as he would have liked.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it,” Mr. Trump said of his trip.

David Pierson contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Auctions 31.5 Million Acres of Pacific Ocean to Deep Sea Mining Company
item.description:
In the first sale of its kind, the Trump administration on Thursday leased 31.5 million acres of the Pacific Ocean to a private deep sea mining company, despite a judge’s ruling this week that the auction would be illegal.

Only one firm bid to lease the seabed, which sits off American Samoa. The $6 million lease would allow the company to do mapping and other preliminary work but not actually mine the ocean floor for metals and minerals.

Administration officials would not disclose the identity of the successful bidder, saying it would be publicly released on Friday.

But Impossible Metals, a San Diego-based deep sea mining firm, had asked the government in April to hold the commercial auction. Company officials did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

The auction took place in Thousand Oaks, Calif., at a fire station near the regional office of the Marine Minerals Administration, a branch of the Interior Department that was created in July. Only two bidders showed up.

Outside the fire station, protesters marched and carried signs opposing the sale.

Deep-sea mining would involve scooping up nodules found on the seafloor that are rich in metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which are important to manufacturing electric cars, batteries and other clean-energy technologies.

But mining the deep ocean has raised global opposition, and environmentalists argue that underwater plumes of sediment stirred up by mining machinery could devastate deep sea ecosystems.

More than 45 countries have called for a ban or pause on seabed mining, which currently does not exist in any commercial form.

But deep sea mining is a priority for President Trump, who last April signed an executive order that instructed the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to expedite approvals for mining companies.

Trump administration officials said the sale would benefit U.S. industries that rely on critical minerals.

“This sale is a critical first step in our offshore energy strategy,” said Michael Olsen, acting director of the Marine Minerals Administration. “It allows us to learn more about the resources in our offshore federal waters, and it enables us to assess whether those resources could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

Whoever the winning bidder is might face an extended legal fight to start prospecting for those deep sea nodules.

On Monday, Judge Jill Otake of the U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service “did not even attempt to consider” the potential harms to endangered marine species when it approved the planned sale, violating the Endangered Species Act. Mr. Trump nominated Judge Otake to the bench in 2017.

The proposed mining area is adjacent to the Rose Atoll National Marine Monument, a 13,500-square mile protected area known for its fragile pink-colored coral reefs, nesting areas for sea turtles, whales and other marine mammals, and more than 250 species of fish and seabirds.

Environmental groups said that the winner of the bid will face difficulty in pursuing a lease that has been ruled unlawful.

“There are a lot of problems with this sale,” said Erik Van de Stouwe, senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council. “The investors of this bidder should ask a lot of hard questions given the court’s recent ruling.”

The N.R.D.C., Earthjustice and Finafinau, a youth-group based in American Samoa, sued the Marine Minerals Administration on Wednesday in federal court in Hawaii, asking the court to strike down any leases that the agency awards.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, said that although the mining lease is outside territorial waters of American Samoa, mining on the seafloor will stir up sediment and other pollution that spreads beyond the immediate area.

“We’re talking about sediment plumes, we’re talking about impacts on marine ecosystems that we completely don’t understand,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said in an interview. “How is that going to affect our corals. How is that going to affect other ecosystems that are already in place?”

Suluai-Mahuka said that many of the 49,000 island residents depend on the commercial tuna industry for their livelihood. They also depend on the ocean for their food. Both are at risk from commercial mining activity, she said.

“At a basic family level, we depend on whether or not we can feed ourselves from the ocean,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said. “You will see families fishing often, and eating the fish that they catch — it’s a daily way of people being able to feed their families. That hasn’t actually been factored in, either.”

American Samoa banned deep sea mining in 2024, citing “significant risks” to marine biodiversity, however its elected officials are split on the issue. On Monday, Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, said he supported the sale.

“Today, we stand at the threshold of a new era of exploration, one that could unlock scientific knowledge, create economic opportunities, and strengthen American Samoa’s role in America’s strategic future in the Pacific,” the governor said in a statement.

Delegate Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen, a Republican who represents the U.S. territory in the U.S. House, called the Monday ruling against the sale “significant” and said that she would reintroduce legislation to ban deep sea mining near American Samoa.

“We treasure our beautiful shores and waters, and we rely on a healthy ocean for fishing,” Ms. Radewagen said in an email to The Times.

item.title: Love and Carjackings in a Video Game
item.description:
Full disclosure: I don’t play video games. I have never played video games. I did read a novel about video games once! (“Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow,” by Gabrielle Zevin. It’s good.)

But even I haven’t been able to avoid the cultural juggernaut that is Grand Theft Auto VI. This week, the legendary franchise released a new game after a 13-year hiatus, and it’s fair to characterize the response as rapturous. “The most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed,” one critic said. “The year’s signature cultural event,” one of our reporters wrote. Some are expecting the first week’s sales to approach $2 billion. “G.T.A. flu” — people planning to stay home from work or school to play — is a thing.

And so I called up my colleague Zachary Small, who reports on arts and culture (and also plays Grand Theft Auto). I wanted to ask him about the blockbuster cultural phenomenon known as G.T.A.

Zach, I am possibly the farthest thing from this game’s target audience. So explain to me: What’s the deal with Grand Theft Auto?

Today we think of Grand Theft Auto as very American, but it actually has roots in Scotland. It was this British take, in the form of a video game, on American crime movies — but the creators realized it’s a lot more fun to play as the bad guys than the good guys.

The Grand Theft Auto we know today unleashes players to wreak havoc across various fictional cities. You can steal cars. You can run over pedestrians. You can do a drug deal or get into a shootout with the police.

So what’s fun about it is that you can do crazy stuff that you can’t do in real life?

You’re thinking about it in the right way. But if you want a more philosophical spin on it, you could say that Grand Theft Auto is also commentary — that it offers this kind of satirical perspective on American culture, and what it means to try to achieve the American dream.

[Our colleague Joseph Bernstein has a great piece about how G.T.A. has always been a cartoonish parody of the United States — and how reality has now outrun the joke.]

Historically, there’s been a lot of pushback from educators and politicians against G.T.A. What were they worried about?

So a lot of the initial controversy around Grand Theft Auto was the developers’ own doing. It’s been reported that when the original came out in 1997, they paid P.R. companies to reach out to British tabloids and say, “Boy, this is a really controversial game; it’s super violent.” And, of course, that had the effect of making people want to play.

But later on, in the post-9/11 period, there were these fears about whether we’d become a violent society. And a lot of those fears became focused on video games and specifically Grand Theft Auto. And it became this sort of moral panic, based on research that today has been largely debunked.

You don’t really hear much of this in the response to G.T.A. VI.

Right, and I think that’s because this release comes at a moment when gaming as an industry is a lot more respected. The game is set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City, and real elected officials in Miami are totally embracing it. The last time a G.T.A. was set in Vice City, there were protests and a lawsuit in Miami. So, there’s been this complete 180.

Why is that?

The series has been around for almost 30 years. A lot of people, including government officials, grew up playing these games, and feel nostalgia for them.

The game itself has also matured in this latest release. G.T.A. had been criticized for misogyny; one of the lead characters this time is a woman who is just as complex as her male counterpart. There’s romance. And, in addition to carjacking people, you can have your character engage in home repairs. So that’s one part of it.

The other part is the quality of these games, which is undeniable. The detail and the realism of G.T.A. VI is incredible.

Think about it this way. This game involves a lot of walking on the beach. Now think about how your foot hits the sand when you’re walking on the beach and how all the tiny pebbles move around as a result. For an animator, how many hours of work does that take? How much work just so a character can lean against a wall? Think about the physics of the clothes a character is wearing as he leans.

Now, think about the fact that in G.T.A. VI, you can go to the beach, and see different scenes unfolding everywhere you look. You can see a dog running into a wave. You can see people hitting a beach ball back and forth. And all of it looks incredibly realistic. The amount of work that takes cannot be overstated. All these thousands of tiny details have been taken into account by a team of almost 5,000 people, with a budget of more than $1 billion.

item.title: Some Very Rare Cats Are Feeling the Heat in Turkey
item.description:
Outside, the sun beat down on the snow-capped mountains that ring the eastern Turkish city of Van. Inside the Van Cat Research Center on a November afternoon, the air-conditioning was on full blast — just to help a roomful of silky white felines keep their cool.

With their striking mismatched eyes of blue and amber, Turkish Van cats are the pampered royalty of the city that shares their name. They’re celebrated in local folklore, honored by a giant statue on the city’s main drag and protected by the Turkish government.

Yet, these iconic cats are feeling the heat. As climate change warms eastern Anatolia, the chief caretaker at the center said finding ways to beat the heat was now nearly a year-round concern.

“We never used to use air-conditioning here,” said Dr. Abdullah Kaya, a veterinarian and professor of biology who directs the research center, which is part of Van Yuzuncu Yil University. “But eventually, because of the rising temperatures, we had to install it,” he said.

Dr. Kaya called Van cats “cold climate animals,” and added, “In the past, the warm season was very short, but now it lasts much longer, and we’ve seen changes in both their skin and their fur.”

The center has successfully rescued the breed from the brink of extinction; fewer than 100 purebred Van cats could be identified in the 1990s. Today, more than 300 roam the facility.

Climate change is warming the eastern Anatolia region of Turkey faster than the global average, according to the United Nations climate science body. Van sits about 5,700 feet above sea level, a bit higher than Denver, and is seeing warmer winters, shrinking snowpack, irregular rainfall patterns and more frequent summer heat waves.

Lake Van, Turkey’s largest lake, also is experiencing an accelerating water crisis driven by shifting weather patterns combined with water mismanagement, said Caner Yerli, an associate professor of agricultural science at Yuzuncu Yil University. Climate modeling shows the Van basin is transitioning toward a hotter, drier Mediterranean-type climate, he noted.

The Van cats are built for harsh Anatolian winters, hence their longish, cashmere-like fur. Dr. Kaya said he has seen worrisome trends. The cats’ coats are thinning more severely in the summer. He’s also noticed significant appetite loss in the summer heat, causing the cats to lose weight.

But the Van breed has one climate adaptation option not available to other felines: their most un-catlike enthusiasm for swimming.

Over the years they have been observed paddling and even diving into Lake Van. Their fur has an unusual texture that repels moisture, like a natural parka that also helps keep them dry in damp or snowy conditions.

Now, when the weather is hot, they swim in specially designed pools at the research center.

“The pools can help reduce the effects of the heat, but of course, the real problem is that climate change is happening too quickly,” Dr. Kaya said. “We need to slow it down.”

The Van cat evolved over centuries in isolation in eastern Anatolia. They gained fame in the 1950s when two Britons writing about Turkey became enamored of them. In the late 1960s, the Van cat was officially recognized as a breed.

Around the same time, rapid urbanization in Turkey was replacing garden homes with multistory apartment buildings, eliminating much of their natural habitat. Some believed Van cats could not live in apartments and abandoned them. Purebred Van cats increasingly crossbred with domestic cats.

By 1992, a survey found only 92 pure Van cats remaining in the Lake Van region, prompting the state-backed university conservation program and government restrictions on taking them out of the country.

The push to save the Van cat is fueled by Turkey’s deep cultural affinity for felines. Here, street cats are neighborhood fixtures and treated like local V.I.P.s. They nap on shop counters, stroll through mosques, sun themselves on Byzantine walls and hop rides on ferries across the Bosporus. They’ve also made Turkey a font of viral online cat content.

There was Yesim, the tabby who became famous for waiting patiently in line at a butcher shop for his daily handout of offal, and Gli, the cross-eyed resident of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul who once charmed Barack Obama.

More recently, a stray ginger stole the show when it interrupted a performance of the “Romeo and Juliet” ballet by Prokofiev.

Yet while ordinary cats roam freely, purebred Van cats have become far too precious to leave to the elements. Today, they are rarely seen wandering the streets and instead almost all lounge indoors.

Dr. Kaya said his center has not been able to conduct a scientific study on how rising temperatures are affecting the breed, though he hopes to find a partner to pursue such research. Meanwhile, he said, the air-conditioned sanctuary offers a sobering warning for Turkey’s street cats.

“Even these cats, which live in a protected and controlled environment, are suffering from the heat,” he said, adding, “Imagine how much harder it must be for cats living outside without any protection.”

Ecehan Sirali translated interviews from the Turkish for this article.

item.title: Devilish or Delightful? Krampus Is Banned From a Christmas Parade.
item.description:
The only reason Tanya Griffin put Krampus in her town’s Christmastime parade last year was because Santa was already taken. So too was the Grinch, and Jack Skellington from “The Nightmare Before Christmas.”

Instead, Ms. Griffin, the owner of a tattoo shop in Strathroy, Ontario, made a float for the local Santa Claus parade starring a shaggy and horn-wearing Krampus, St. Nicholas’s evil accomplice in central European folklore. Ms. Griffin won second place for costumes, and this year she was striving for first.

Then she found out organizers were banning her float.

The Lions Club in Strathroy said it had banned Ms. Griffin’s display from its annual parade on Saturday because it was worried that “scary costumes, rattling chains and beating sticks” would frighten children. Ms. Griffin, 43, said the concerns were overblown — and come at the cost of inclusion in a small town.

“It’s not just the float. It’s the culture,” Ms. Griffin said, referring to people of German descent who live in the area. “It’s the dismissal of an entire group of people.”

Other recent Krampus appearances have drawn controversy. Last year, a parade float in Hawaii generated criticism, while in 2024 the Archdiocese of San Antonio condemned a Krampus parade for the figure’s “resemblance to the devil.”

Krampus, frequently depicted with a whip and wearing animal skins, traces its roots to the alpine winters of Austria, Germany and nearby countries, according to Heide Castañeda, a professor of anthropology at the University of South Florida who has studied identity and rituals for 25 years.

In folklore, the monster appears alongside St. Nicholas, punishing children who misbehave. While its horns often remind people of Satan, Ms. Castañeda said Krampus had distinct origins.

Now, the figure is having a moment. Helped by social media and pop culture exposure, including a 2015 movie, Krampus clubs have sprung up across North America, organizing events and helping preserve traditions associated with Krampus. Ms. Castañeda is set to speak at the inaugural Krampus America convention in February in Florida.

“There’s been a huge resurgence in the last 20, 25 years in these traditions,” she said.

Strathroy, roughly halfway between Detroit and Toronto, is home to about 20,000 residents. Its annual Santa Claus parade, partly funded by the town, has been running for more than six decades. Locals pack downtown streets every year, said Daniel Kiekens, a real estate agent and chairman of the Strathroy Business Improvement Area.

Ms. Griffin, who owns Coven House Tattoos and Piercings in Strathroy, learned about Krampus when she was young — her birthday falls on Krampusnacht, when, according to folklore, Krampus deals with the world’s naughty.

She decided the monster was a perfect fit for the parade last year, which she said also featured floats from Starbucks and a local Pride group. “It’s not all babies and mangers,” she added.

Ms. Griffin said she received a letter last year from the nearby Calvary Pentecostal Church after Krampus appeared in the parade wearing a Santa suit, horns and ghoulish mask.

In the letter, shared by Ms. Griffin, the congregation wrote that it was disgusted by the “inclusion of satanic influences into what should have been a Christ-centered” parade.

“The Municipality of Strathroy-Caradoc must be aware of the damage these demonic forces would have on the young children of our town,” the congregation wrote.

The church did not respond to email and phone messages.

The Strathroy Lions Club said in a statement that it had dismissed the complaints it received from “certain religious groups,” but said that it had banned her float this year because Ms. Griffin had sought to “recruit a crowd of people to march through the streets, scaring people and causing chaos.”

Ms. Griffin said she had planned to have children and parents walk alongside the Krampus float wearing cloaks and antlers. She said she had also arranged for a Norwegian caroler to sing traditional alpine songs.

The club said Ms. Griffin’s float was welcome to join the parade if it was the same as last year’s.

Instead, Ms. Griffin is planning a meet-and-greet with Krampus at her tattoo shop, which sits on the parade route. She will hand out candy, temporary tattoos and coal. She expects people to dress up as Krampus in protest of the float’s omission. She said the police have told her the environment could get tense.

Jonathan Mintz, an artist at Ms. Griffin’s shop who will play Krampus, was born in Strathroy and attended the Santa Claus parade every year growing up. This year promises to be different. “It sounds like it’s going to be crazy down here,” Mr. Mintz said.

Mr. Kiekens, chair of the Strathroy business association, said he hadn’t heard complaints from local businesses about the controversy. But it has gotten people in town talking.

“Strathroy getting on the map,” he said. “Now, I’m not sure that’s what we want to be on the map for.”

item.title: Chinese-Born Neuroscientist Is Detained by ICE While Traveling From Conference
item.description:
A Chinese-born neuroscientist conducting research at Princeton University was detained on Thursday by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Washington while traveling from an academic conference, university officials and her lawyers said.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, is a third year Ph.D. student who has resided in the United States since 2016. Her visa was expired, her lawyers said, but her pending asylum application allowed her to remain in the country legally.

Via the messaging platform Slack, she informed her colleagues at Princeton’s Brody Lab that she had been detained at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while traveling home to New Jersey. But her lab mates eventually lost direct contact with her.

As of Friday, Ms. Xie was being held at an ICE processing center in Chantilly, Va. She is the latest in a string of foreign-born scientists who have been detained amid Trump administration crackdowns on foreign scientists and on immigrants more broadly.

Those policies have had a chilling effect on American research institutions’ ability to recruit and retain the world’s top minds, creating a strain on fields already struggling to enroll young researchers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” said Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

After Ms. Xie moved to the United States with her family in 2016, she went on to graduate in 2020 from the Bronx High School of Science and in 2024 from M.I.T., where she studied computer science and mathematics. Since then, she has lived in New Jersey while conducting neuroscience research as a Ph.D. student at the Brody Lab.

Earlier this week, Ms. Xie presented some of this research — on the neurons that act as a coordinate system for the brain’s mental maps — at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting in Washington.

“Eva is a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist,” the Brody Lab said in a statement on X. “She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center. She should be home.”

According to Ms. Xie’s lawyers, because her asylum application has not yet been approved and her previous visa is expired, ICE agents were alerted when she passed through an airport security checkpoint.

“In her case, as well as a number of other cases that I personally represent, we’ve seen people being arrested at domestic airports who’ve overstayed a visa but have a pending green card or asylum application,” said Kerry Doyle, one of Ms. Xie’s attorneys.

Officials from ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the grounds for Ms. Xie’s detention or whether she had been moved from the Virginia processing facility.

On Friday morning, Ms. Xie’s lawyers entered a habeas corpus filing, which formally requests that the court review whether a person’s detention is legal.

Princeton confirmed that it had arranged for Ms. Xie to receive legal counsel and would remain in contact with her attorneys, family and colleagues as the situation developed. The Society for Neuroscience said in a statement that it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to offer support.

“Our thoughts are with Eva, her family and her colleagues,” the society said in a statement on X.

item.title: Denmark Expels Russian Diplomat After Accusing Moscow of Planning a Hit
item.description:
Denmark ordered Russia’s defense attaché to leave the country after it accused Moscow on Friday of orchestrating a plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper at a concert near Copenhagen in late September.

Danish intelligence officials said Russian operatives had enlisted members of a notorious Danish gang to carry out the killing.

“It is an outrageous and completely unacceptable violation of our boundaries, and it calls for a clear response,” Denmark’s foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, said Friday. The government was “absolutely certain,” he said, that Russian intelligence services were behind the plot, though he did not provide details.

The case comes amid growing concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and espionage across Europe. Germany has linked Moscow to a planned attack involving an explosive-laden drone, while unexplained drone incidents have disrupted Danish airports.

This, according to Danish intelligence officials, is the first known Russian assassination attempt on Danish soil.

The intended target was Kyivstoner, a 34-year-old Ukrainian-American rapper whose real name is Albert Vasiliev. Known for his playful humor, comedy sketches and bass-heavy hip-hop, Kyivstoner has built a following in both Ukraine and Russia while occasionally wading into politics. He has condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine but has also criticized the Ukrainian government’s handling of military mobilization.

In a statement, the Russian Embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations as “absurd” and accused Denmark of providing no evidence while staging a “propaganda show.”

The embassy belittled Kyivstoner, saying he had “insignificant political influence and questionable fame.” The statement accused the Danish authorities of routinely maligning Moscow, saying a “Danish model” has emerged in which even the most implausible events were given an alleged “Russian connection.”

In July, Russia’s security service, the FSB, accused Kyivstoner of helping smuggle drones into Russia for an attack near Moscow, an allegation he denies. A month later, the Polish authorities said they foiled a Russian-backed plot to kill him, arresting a Russian suspect.

On Sept. 25, Kyivstoner was scheduled to perform at an old inn in an affluent suburb of Copenhagen. Minutes before the concert was to begin, Danish police intercepted a car carrying four men about two kilometers from the venue.

Inside, the authorities said, the officers found two loaded pistols and two knives. The men were arrested, and the concert was canceled.

All four have remained in custody since September in connection with weapons charges. Two now also face charges of attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Prosecutors said the suspects received instructions from Russian intelligence services, took steps to attend the concert and obtained the weapons before driving to the venue.

Danish officials said that the suspects were members of Loyal to Familia, a banned Danish gang known for violent crime, and that senior gang members helped plan the attack.

“Russian intelligence services are both willing and able to carry out assassination attempts here, at public events, using people from Denmark’s criminal underworld,” Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, Denmark’s domestic intelligence chief, said Friday. He said the case reflected an increasingly aggressive Russia willing to take greater risks.

Danish officials said that they would give Russia’s defense attaché a week to pack up and that they would push other European countries to stop issuing nonessential visas to Russians.

“We will not be intimidated,” said Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister. “Never bend. Never waver from what we believe in.”

item.title: White Police Officers Are Convicted of Beating a Black Man in France
item.description:
Three white police officers were convicted by a Paris court on Friday of beating a Black man in 2020 and forging a police report that wrongly incriminated him, in a case that spurred a national outcry about police conduct.

The judges who issued the verdict cited racism as an aggravating circumstance of the assault, even though the investigative judges who conducted the pretrial investigation had decided not to make it a criminal charge.

Two were sentenced to jail and the third to house arrest, and all were banned from police work. In their trial, they had acknowledged that they had assaulted and falsely accused the man, Michel Zecler, a music producer, but denied racist intent.

Serge Money, one of Mr. Zecler’s lawyers, told journalists the verdict was “a turning point,” allowing victims of police brutality to “go forward with confidence, since they can now rely on what must be called the Zecler precedent.”

The episode occurred in November 2020 after the officers stopped Mr. Zecler, now 47, to check his identity outside his studio, in part because he had contravened pandemic restrictions by not wearing a face mask. The officers ended up beating him inside his studio for several minutes.

Mr. Zecler was held in custody for two days, accused of resisting arrest, but released without charge after security camera footage showed the officers punching, kicking and beating him with a baton, without his retaliating. The officers were identified in court as Aurélien Lapersonne, Philippe Tondeux and Pierre Plantier.

At the time, footage of the assault fueled a political crisis in France and resonated globally, months after the murder of George Floyd and worldwide Black Lives Matter protests.

When it finally began six years later, the rare trial of police officers unfolded as France’s security forces faced renewed scrutiny over more accusations of brutality in response to a youth-led protest movement that has rocked the country since September.

During the trial, Mr. Zecler expressed frustration that it had taken so long for the officers to face justice. “Even with the power of the images, it took six years and then six days of trial to get the beginning of an admission from my attackers about the system that led them to lie in order to protect themselves,” Mr. Zecler said on social media.

He was hit 31 times inside his studio, according to an overview of the case by investigative judges.

Doctors said he suffered a wound to his left arm that damaged a tendon and required surgery, as well as a head injury and wounds to his scalp and lower lip, all of which incapacitated him for at least 45 days.

Mr. Zecler said this month to the French news site Loopsider, which published footage of his assault six years ago, that it had caused him “colossal damage.”

“After the punches, there’s still a lot of anger left, I think,” he said. “Why did they do that? Why did it happen that way? In reality, that’s what I really want to know.”

Though Mr. Zecler said the officers had called him racist slurs, they denied accusations of racism, and investigative judges ruled there was not enough evidence to charge them with racist intent.

But the investigative judges noted that an examination of Mr. Lapersonne’s phone had revealed “a number of remarks and jokes in truly poor taste, reflecting a number of biases based on ethnic origin.”

In its verdict, the trial court considered racism as an aggravating factor in the crimes.

There is no official tally of episodes of police brutality against Black or Arab people in France, mainly because the country forbids collecting official data on race. But in 2017, an independent official body found that young men perceived as Black or Arab were 20 times as likely to have their identities checked.

In Mr. Zecler’s case, the court found that the officers had illegally entered his private premises, the studio, without permission. Testifying in court on Tuesday, they said the incident unfolded too fast for them to understand that.

The officers said they were overcome by fear, after then finding themselves stuck in a narrow space with Mr. Zecler. They maintained that they were unable to subdue him, and had heard more individuals moving nearby.

Mr. Tondeux described the officers’ violence as “a failure,” and Mr. Plantier apologized to Mr. Zecler.

Mr. Lapersonne, who initiated the arrest, said he could not justify the six punches that he had thrown at Mr. Zecler outside his studio, but attempted to defend punching the producer inside the studio. He said he had tried and failed to subdue Mr. Zecler in a chokehold, and felt his life and those of his two colleagues had been endangered.

He said he had filed a false report of the arrest, incorrectly stating that Mr. Zecler had hit the officers, because at the time he believed that to be true.

The other two officers said they had signed off on Mr. Lapersonne’s report without thoroughly reviewing it, and filed separate complaints against Mr. Zecler because their superior suggested they do so.

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

item.title: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Woman Drugged by Husband
item.description:
Four British men were found guilty on Thursday of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged her and secretly arranged for strangers to rape her while she was incapacitated.

It is the first time in England that a jury has convicted multiple defendants relating to drug-facilitated sexual assault.

The abuse of the woman, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity under British law, spanned more than 13 years. Her husband, Philip Young, a former elected local official in the southwestern English borough of Swindon, pleaded guilty to 48 offenses, including 11 counts of rape, according to the Crown Prosecution Service.

Speaking after the jury’s verdict against the four men in the Winchester Crown Court on Thursday, Ms. Young said it sent a message to women and girls: that it is possible to “be believed and understood” in the British criminal justice system.

“It’s a relief not just for me and my family, but a relief for what this means for other women in the future,” she said. “It means that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward.”

Two of the defendants were convicted of rape, and the other two of sexual assault. Sentencing was scheduled for December.

Mr. Young solicited the other men online, using platforms like Craigslist and Grindr, and arranged for them to visit the couple’s home in Swindon. In three of the four men’s cases, prosecutors had video evidence, filmed by Mr. Young, of Ms. Young drugged, blindfolded and restrained as the abuse took place.

The four men argued in court that they had believed that Ms. Young had consented to the encounters based on assurances from her husband. The jury found that was not enough, and that the defendants — Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni, and Mohammed Hassan — had failed to establish legal consent.

Ms. Young’s case echoed that of Gisèle Pelicot, the Frenchwoman whose husband also drugged and raped her repeatedly and invited dozens of men into their bedroom to do the same. That abuse began in 2010, but Ms. Pelicot did not learn of it until 2020.

She decided to come forward, prompting a national reckoning in France, and inspiring women across the country to rally around her and demand a change to the country’s consent laws. In 2024, 51 defendants were found guilty of assaulting her.

item.title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds
item.description:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that makes the Southeast Asian nation the first state to be held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ruling covers Myanmar’s deadly military campaign against the Rohingya minority, which killed at least 10,000 people in a few weeks in 2017 and forced three quarters of a million people to flee during that same period. More deaths and expulsions followed.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine state,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the I.C.J., said while reading the court’s decision on Thursday. The decision was made by 9 votes to 6.

The decision could have sweeping implications, including for another genocide case before the I.C.J., the United Nations’ highest judicial body: the accusation of genocide by Israel against the people of the Gaza Strip.

A spokeswoman for the government of Myanmar, in the capital Naypyidaw, did not answer a phone call seeking comment after the verdict was handed down. Myanmar authorities have previously disputed the charge.

Among other findings, the court determined that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocide. While it was not found to have incited private people to commit genocide, the court found that it also failed to punish genocide.

“This is a case a decade in the making,” said Juliette McIntyre, a Senior Lecturer in Law at Adelaide University in Australia. “From the point of view of the Rohingya people, who have been waiting, and waiting, and waiting for justice, this is very important.”

Gambia filed suit against Myanmar in 2019 in the court, which is based in The Hague. While the West African country is thousands of miles from Myanmar, international law gives countries the ability to act against genocide anywhere in the world — even if they are not affected.

In the Jamtoli camp of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, people thronged to a public viewing party to watch the hourslong decision, cheering and weeping as the decision was read. Some held signs that said “thank you, Gambia.”

In The Hague, Dawda Jallow, the attorney general for Gambia, welcomed the decision to find Myanmar culpable of the “crime of crimes.” Speaking to journalists on the main staircase of the I.C.J.’s Peace Palace shortly after the ruling was read, he said, “we will stand with the Rohingya until justice is served.”

The violence at the core of the case took place in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine state, starting in 2016 and worsening in 2017. U.N. officials and human rights groups have called it a coordinated, scorched-earth campaign to remove the Rohingya — one that involved killing, wounding and raping, razing villages, and eventually forcing the expulsion of more than a million people to neighboring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Muslims have a long history of repression in Myanmar. After the nation’s independence from Britain in 1948, they were one of many ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. But over time, they faced increasing attacks from members of the nation’s Buddhist majority.

A restrictive citizenship law in 1982 effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. Various Myanmar governments, including a civilian authority led by the Nobel peace laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, falsely referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s military called its campaign against the Rohingya “clearance operations.” Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi defended the military at the I.C.J., denying it committed genocide, before her government was deposed by the military and she was imprisoned in 2021. (After the coup, Myanmar descended into a civil war that is still raging.) About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in dire conditions in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. Following the eruption of Myanmar’s civil war in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a milita from the Rakhine ethnic minority, which has also been accused of persecuting Rohingya.

Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.

The court found that Myanmar took measures to wipe out the Rohingya people, who did constitute a protected ethnic group by the court’s judgment.

The case summary states that, among other atrocities, the court found that “widespread acts of extreme violence were perpetrated by the Myanmar security forces against children in northern Rakhine State,” that “in addition to the extreme hardship of the journey, the Myanmar security forces systematically shot at Rohingya as they were fleeing,” and that “the evidence demonstrates a deliberate, organized process” of destroying Rohingya villages.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Iwasawa read from the ruling.

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution — trying to put things back as they were, including through allowing return and reunification — and, where that fails, compensation. But the amount of compensation needed is not yet set, and will be determined in further proceedings.

The court does not have the power to enforce its own rulings, and the U.N. Security Council would need to uphold the decision. Two members of the Security Council, China and Russia, may opt to protect Myanmar. Each provides Myanmar with weapons it now uses to kill civilians in the civil war.

“Concerned governments” should “press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said in a written statement following the announcement.

Notably, the United States has previously said that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, though that happened during the Biden administration.

“I think that you’re going to see relatively powerful states putting pressure on Myanmar,” said Ms. McIntyre, of Adelaide University. “How much they pay heed to that pressure is a question.”

Thursday’s decision was greeted by some in the international legal community as a sign that justice can still be served on a global stage, even as the Trump administration attacks international bodies. The administration plans to impose sweeping sanctions against another tribunal, the International Criminal Court, which could severely impair the court’s ability to function on a day-to-day basis.

“At a moment when international law and the institutions that uphold it face growing pressure, the Court’s decision reaffirms the vital role they play in establishing truth,” James Goldston, the executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.

For the Rohingya now in Bangladesh, the news was welcome. Yet tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

Mohammed Yeasin said his wife and sister were killed in a drone attack in August 2024. The perpetrators were not the Myanmar military but the armed group from the Rakhine ethnic minority that shares its homeland with the Rohingya.

“I am happy about the I.C.J.,” he said. “But I don’t know when my sorrows will end.”

Jonathan Wolfe, Marlise Simons and Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

item.title: Wreck of First Australian-Built Warship Is Revealed 128 Years After It Sank
item.description:
Maritime archaeologists and navy divers have located the wreck of the first Australian warship 128 years after it sank, Australia’s Defense Department announced this week.

The authorities and scholars said the discovery of the wooden gunboat, Spitfire, was particularly significant because it was the first warship to be built in Australia in the 1800s under the British colonial government. The ship was constructed in Sydney and launched in 1855. It sank during a cyclone more than 40 years later near the Piper Islands in the Great Barrier Reef.

The wreck site of the 52-foot vessel, made of ironbark and blackwood with copper fastenings, was located in August off the northern state of Queensland after a monthlong expedition that involved a minehunter vessel, remotely operated vehicles and a navy dive team.

An “acoustic anomaly” caused by the wreck was detected by a sonar team, leading to the discovery, the announcement said. Clearance divers with the Australian Navy, specialists who typically deal with underwater demolitions and explosive ordinance removal, then documented the parts of the wreck that were exposed above the seabed, according to maritime archaeologists involved in the search.

Spitfire was commissioned by the state government of New South Wales, where Sydney is located, to protect the city against Russian warships based in Vladivostok, according to the Australian navy. After serving as a patrol boat and pilot vessel, the ship was sold off into private ownership and was used in commercial fishing in the trade for bêche-de-mer, or sea cucumbers.

The site of the wreck is protected as underwater cultural heritage under Australian law.

item.title: After Brexit, Baby Steps to Bre-entry? What to Expect at U.K.-E.U. Summit
item.description:
British and European leaders are set to meet in Brussels on Friday to remove some barriers introduced by Brexit, a decade after U.K. voters decided to leave the now 27-nation bloc.

The reset has been reinvigorated by Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who declared this week that Brexit “has not worked.” “It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes, where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth,” Mr. Burnham said in a speech Monday, adding: “To be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years.”

Many hurdles stand between Britain and a dramatically closer relationship with Brussels, but officials are slowly chipping away at their differences. This is the second summit focused on closer collaboration.

Here’s what to watch for.

The goals of the one-day summit are specific, and fairly modest. They are the result of months of diplomatic work that began when the previous Labour prime minister, Keir Starmer, entered office and began pursuing closer ties with Europe. They include:

An agreement to relax restrictions on agricultural trade. This would help British farmers, who have complained since Brexit about the paperwork required to sell goods to the E.U.

A “youth experience” program. This would allow tens of thousands of young people in Europe to temporarily work and study in Britain — and vice versa — without the restrictions put in place after Brexit.

A deal to realign their carbon emissions trading systems, with a goal of making it easier and cheaper for businesses to deal with environmental regulations.

Some changes introduced after Brexit are not being discussed:

Freedom of movement is still off the table. Britons and Europeans used to have quicker and easier checks at one another’s borders. And European and British workers cannot move between jobs in Britain and on the continent as easily as they could before Brexit.

Trade talks remain different. Britain negotiates and strikes its own trade deals post-Brexit, whereas in the European Union, trade policy is made by the bloc.

In Britain, the shift in tone is coming from the top.

“After 10 years,” said Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist at Johns Hopkins, “there is a prime minister who is prepared to recognize openly what everyone has known for 10 years: that Brexit was a huge, excuse my Oxford English” — finishing the thought with an expletive.

That opens the door to a serious conversation about the future of Britain’s relationship with the European Union, she said.

The reset is also heavily informed by three countries not in the room.

President Trump has spent two years upending global trade with tariffs, prodding Europe to take more responsibility for its own defense, cozying up to Russia and surprising allies. That has pushed America’s closest partners to look for friends elsewhere.

Europe and Britain both face economic risks from China’s exports and the race between the Chinese and the United States for artificial intelligence dominance. And Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine has underscored the need for defense preparedness.

Britain’s E.U. reset is “a reaction to Donald Trump, but not only: It’s also about a recognition that in a less rules-based world, you need to have a critical mass,” said Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive of the European Policy Center, a think tank.

Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons now think Brexit was a mistake. But even some Labour officials admit they are wary of another acrimonious debate.

They also fear that moving closer to Europe could benefit Nigel Farage, the pro-Brexit leader of Reform U.K., and Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the Conservative Party. Both politicians are eager to revive the fights over immigration and British sovereignty that powered the Leave campaign.

Even those who support closer ties between the bloc and the U.K. suggest that nothing about a second political marriage will be easy.

“When Brexit was decided on by a referendum, there was a lack of clarity as to what exactly that meant,” Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador to Britain, said at an event at Chatham House in London this week. That makes it hard to negotiate.

While Mr. Burnham has cracked the door open to Britain possibly rejoining the bloc one day, he insists that he will only present options to the public, and that any decision would take place after the next general election. “At every stage, the British people will be the boss,” he said.

Any move to rejoin the European Union — or even just the customs union, or a bespoke and close relationship that looks more like the one the bloc has with Switzerland — could take years. It took more than five for Britain to leave.

It is also unclear how the bloc would approach a bid to rejoin, especially following a series of elections next year.

“As much as people might miss the U.K., there is also very much a sense of: Well, you’ve left, and we’ve had to get on with it,” said Rebecca Christie, a senior fellow at Bruegel, a research institute.

Megan Specia contributed reporting.
